chunks: Abu al-Husayn Ahmad ibn Abdullah ibn Ali al-Naqid narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Rahman al-Balkhi [al-Sulami] narrated to me, and Abu al-Husayn said to me, and my uncle informed me from his father from Abu Nasr from a man from the people of Bayt al-Maqdis, that he said:

By Allah, we, the people of Bayt al-Maqdis and its suburbs, knew of the killing of al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon him) on the eve of the day he was killed. I asked, 'How did you know?' He replied: 'We did not lift a stone, a clod of earth, or a rock without seeing fresh, boiling blood beneath it. And the walls turned red like blood. It rained fresh blood for three days. And we heard a caller crying out in the depth of the night, saying: Does the nation that killed Husayn hope for the intercession of his grandfather on the Day of Reckoning? Far be it from Allah! You will not attain certainty. The intercession of Ahmad and Abu Turab. You killed the best of those who rode beasts, and the best of the gray-haired and the youth. And the sun was eclipsed for three days, then it cleared from it, and the stars became interlocked. And when it was the next day, we were shaken by his killing, and not much time had passed until the news of al-Husayn (peace be upon him) came to us.'

key_terms.أَبُو تُرَابٍ: Abu Turab (a title of Imam Ali)

ai.seo_question: What were the signs of Imam Husayn's death in Jerusalem according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Ibn Qulawayh’s *Kamil al-Ziyarat* highlights the cosmological resonance of Imam al-Husayn’s martyrdom, illustrating the Shia belief that the heavens and earth mourn the Ahl al-Bayt. The specific mention of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) as a witness underscores the universal scope of the event, while the celestial caller’s poem emphasizes the exclusion of the killers from the Prophet’s intercession due to their betrayal.
